issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger profile mixes tactile/startle-type cues and driving-with-others cues that could fit war-zone trauma, but 'being looked at sexually' points toward a sexual-threat trauma context that is not supported elsewhere in memory, threat, or appraisal items. This specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The dominant threat items describe generalized vigilance and fear of interpersonal attack. In combination with the sexual-objectification trigger, this pulls the profile toward an interpersonal/sexual trauma formulation, whereas the memory and appraisal items do not contain corresponding themes. This creates cross-node incoherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear link to the other selected items. The rest of the appraisals center on unfairness, shame, and inability to trust oneself; without any role-related trauma content in memory, triggers, or threat, this item feels weakly anchored and clinically mismatched relative to the otherwise war-zone/interpersonal-danger presentation.

vignette:
Mele was a 46-year-old married veterinarian who had spent part of her adult life doing animal health work in a civilian area that became engulfed by armed conflict. She described the day that stayed with her as beginning like many others, moving between frightened families, injured livestock, and the noise of vehicles on damaged roads. She had been traveling with other people when fighting broke out nearby. The sounds were sudden and overwhelming—sharp blasts, shouting, impacts she could not place—and in the crush of bodies someone grabbed at her to pull her down or move her faster. What remained with her was not a single orderly story but a set of jagged moments: the violent noise, the pressure of hands on her before she understood who was touching her, the sensation of being trapped in a vehicle with others while danger was somewhere outside, and the certainty, for those minutes, that she had no control over what would happen next. When she tried to tell it now, the memory did not come out cleanly. It arrived in broken pieces that did not fully join up, then returned again as if a film had started in her mind without her permission.

In the months after returning to the United States, Mele found that ordinary life no longer felt ordinary inside her body. She told herself she was home, married, safe, back to work, yet she moved through her days as though something could break through at any moment. At night she had difficulty falling asleep because part of her felt she had to remain alert. She would lie in bed listening for sounds in the house, the street, the heating system, anything out of place. Even on evenings when she could say plainly that there was no danger around her, she could not relax into that knowledge. Her husband noticed that she startled if he touched her unexpectedly in the kitchen or came up behind her while she was charting, and she would turn sharply before she recognized him. She hated those moments. They left her flushed with embarrassment, already hearing the familiar thought that she could not rely on herself, that when something happened she became disorganized and useless.

The same pattern followed her into her work at the veterinary clinic. Mele was highly experienced and attentive with animals, but she had begun arranging her day in quiet, careful ways. If a technician reached past her without warning while they were restraining a dog or preparing an exam room, her whole body tightened. Loud noises in the clinic—the metallic crash of a dropped tray, a barking eruption from the kennels, a door slamming—could pull her out of what she was doing and leave her scanning the room before she could return to the task. She watched entrances, listened for changes in tone, noticed who was moving where. Colleagues saw her as tense and serious; a few had commented that she seemed unable to settle even during slower shifts. Mele knew it too. She kept looking for danger even when she disliked herself for it.

Driving became another place where the past intruded. She could drive alone, though rigidly, but having other people in the car was much harder. The feeling of sharing an enclosed moving space with others brought back the war-zone ride in a way she could not fully explain. If her husband suggested a longer drive together or friends offered to carpool, she made excuses, took separate cars, or insisted on routes she felt she controlled. Over time these habits narrowed her life. She and her husband went fewer places together, and at work she avoided off-site visits if they involved riding with others. The consequences were practical and relational at once: more strain, more misunderstandings, more private effort spent simply getting through routine situations.

When memories came, they brought not only fear but shame. She felt ashamed remembering how little control she had had, ashamed that she still could not assemble the event into a coherent account, ashamed of the ways she now reacted to touch and sound. She had come to believe that what happened to her was profoundly unfair and that nothing meaningful had been done about it. Just as painful was her conviction that bad things could happen and she would be unable to stop them. In session she did not present this as an abstract belief; it was the conclusion she drew each time her body reacted before her mind caught up.

Mele finally sought help after a loud crash at the clinic and an unannounced touch from behind by a coworker happened within the same afternoon. She spun around, shaken and humiliated, then later sat in her car unable to start driving home with her husband on the phone asking whether he should come get her. She said she was tired of living as if she had to stay on watch everywhere. What frightened her most was the possibility that this was who she was now—someone who could not trust herself, could not relax, and could not keep bad things from happening. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to feel safe in her own life again.
